title: I'm making Velundra, a dark-fantasy MMORPG that runs in the browser (no download, free). Today I shipped 1.2.0 with its third land, the Salt Marshes: a walled harbour town, six zones, levels 26–35, a world boss and a final boss. The video is the devlog of the update.
author: GastonSaillen
selftext:
I'm making **Velundra**, a dark-fantasy MMORPG that runs in the browser (no download, free). Today we shipped 1.2.0 with its third land, **the Salt Marshes**: a walled harbour town, six zones, levels 26–35, a world boss and a final boss. The video is the devlog of the update.

Some numbers, straight from git:

* **9 days** from the first map concept (Nov 15) to release (Nov 24). The first playable version — boat crossing from the previous zone, the town with its NPCs, the beach's monsters and the first two acts of quests — was running **the same day**, about 10 hours after the first concept.
* **356 commits** in those 9 days (219 of them in the zone's own branch); **1,512 commits** in the whole project, which started a month ago.
* What's in it: a 920 × 920 m map, 57 NPCs, 51 monster types, 300 monster groups, 562 hand-placed props, \~90 quests, 10 armour sets, 5 live events and 2 bosses.

**The workflow I use for every new zone:**

1. **Paint it first.** Three layout concepts for the zone (a bay, a long coast, islands and tides). I pick one, and that painting becomes the reference: it's literally what players see when they open the big map.
2. **Trace the painting into data.** Coast, zones, roads, the town's walls and streets go into a layout file. The land follows the painting's shape, not a square.
3. **Check the routes before building anything.** A script walks every road and checks every zone, quest spot and NPC can be reached on foot. Nothing gets built until that passes.
4. **Build it from data.** Terrain, collision grid and decoration are generated from the map JSON with seeded randomness, identically on the server and the client (the server is authoritative and pathfinds everything). Then I hand-place props in an in-house editor, with a "nobody sees this" check that flags anything the camera never shows, so it doesn't cost frames.
5. **Monsters from a concept board.** 3–4 options per creature; I pick one, then it's modelled, rigged and given its own moves. Every common monster also gets a "rotten leader" variant: same body, bigger, decayed texture.
6. **Quests on a time budget.** The zone is paced for \~20 hours, and the story never makes you grind: a script plays the quests at the measured pace and flags anywhere the story would wait for a hunt.
7. **Bots play the whole thing.** Story bots run every quest with both classes, walking, before release; attack bots hammer every server message. They caught a quest that could never be completed — standing on lava counted as "fighting" — on the very day we shipped.
8. **60 FPS from frame 1.** Everything (models, vegetation, merged chunks, shaders) is built behind the loading screen, so walking never stutters.

It's free and runs in any desktop browser: [**https://velundra.io**](https://play.velundra.io) — happy to answer anything about the workflow, the server or the browser side.

comments.author: aigamedev-mod
comments.body: u/GastonSaillen please expand this post with how you used AI during development. It's not enough to say you used AI. Tell us what you did with it. The point of Rule 4 is for promotional posts to give something back by sharing the process and actual development. We're cracking down on posts that only advertise. If you don't update, this may be removed.

comments.author: PM_Me_Those_
comments.body: Stop making it. Not only do we not need more MMOs, we definitely do not need them developed by a single person.

replies.author: maxneuds
replies.body:
\>massive< multiplayer online rpg live from a huge community. Without that it's just a bad rpg in a pool of many good rpgs. And without an actual team doing community management, hype, publishing, support, etc it will be nothing but a shitty rpg.

Also the reality is: Now every day a ton of "mmorpgs" are thrown into the internet and none of these are interesting. No deep story, no interesting art or atmosphere. It's just the next piece of code on a pile of trash.

If you want a good mmo...

1) Build a good game (rpg)

2) Build a huge community and playerbase

3) Now think about creating an mmo for this franchise
